prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val] Extreme · 10 columns + unbreakable values (language en).
Grid: 10 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "ID" · longest unbreakable word 16px · one-line width 16px
  col 2: header "SKU" · longest unbreakable word 44px · one-line width 136px
  col 3: header "Color" · longest unbreakable word 40px · one-line width 40px
  col 4: header "Size" · longest unbreakable word 31px · one-line width 31px
  col 5: header "Qty" · longest unbreakable word 26px · one-line width 26px
  col 6: header "Price" · longest unbreakable word 41px · one-line width 41px
  col 7: header "Tax" · longest unbreakable word 32px · one-line width 32px
  col 8: header "Total" · longest unbreakable word 47px · one-line width 47px
  col 9: header "Warehouse" · longest unbreakable word 81px · one-line width 122px
  col 10: header "Tracking" · longest unbreakable word 159px · one-line width 159px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 720px. You MAY choose a total wider than 719px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Rendering convention: the screenshot always shows the WHOLE table. Anything beyond the dashed box is not clipped; it is the part a reader reaches by scrolling sideways, so judge both what fits in the box at first sight and the cost of scrolling to the rest.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 720px (different strategies, not small variations).
An earlier design attempt for this table was rejected by independent reviewers. Their comments: another layout was rated acceptable: The table fits the viewport, and the numeric columns scan clearly. SKU and warehouse values wrap at hyphens, but tracking identifiers split across lines. | another layout was rated poor: SKU and warehouse values wrap reasonably, but the tracking identifiers extend beyond their column and the viewport, making the table boundary misleading. | another layout was rated bad: Warehouse and Tracking headers split within words, while SKU, warehouse and tracking values fragment over several lines. Wide short-value columns leave little room for the identifiers. | another layout was rated good: Tracking identifiers remain intact and the table fits the viewport. The narrow SKU column forces each identifier onto four lines, creating tall rows. | your previous preferred design was rated poor: The compact SKU and warehouse wrapping supports scanning, but tracking identifiers overflow their column and extend beyond the viewport. | another layout was rated good: SKU and tracking identifiers remain intact, with clear numeric columns and moderate warehouse wrapping. Tracking sits partly beyond the initial viewport and requires horizontal scrolling.
another layout was rated bad: Equal-looking columns leave excess space in short fields while SKU, warehouse names, tracking values, and even headers break across multiple lines. The tall rows are hard to scan. | another layout was rated poor: Most columns scan well, but the tracking values run beyond the viewport and appear to overflow their allocated column. SKU and warehouse values wrap into two lines. | another layout was rated good: The compact fields are proportioned well, and SKU and warehouse values wrap at hyphens. Tracking values split across two lines, but the whole table fits in the viewport. | your previous preferred design was rated poor: The short fields and two-line SKU and warehouse values are readable, but tracking values extend beyond the viewport and appear to overflow their column. | another layout was rated acceptable: SKU values remain intact and the numeric columns scan cleanly. Tracking lies partly beyond the initial viewport, so readers must scroll to see the full identifiers. | another layout was rated acceptable: Tracking values remain intact and the full table fits in the viewport, but the narrow SKU column breaks each identifier into four lines, making rows unnecessarily tall and SKUs harder to compare.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}
